items.stem: State what is meant by the term "labour productivity".
items.answer: Output per worker or per hour worked
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: output per worker or per hour worked. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Briefly explain why growth based only on increases in AD cannot be sustained indefinitely.
items.answer: Once the economy reaches potential output, further AD increases mainly raise the price level; sustained growth requires increases in productive capacity.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Once the economy reaches potential output, further AD increases mainly raise the price level; sustained growth requires increases in productive capacity. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain the difference between actual economic growth and potential economic growth.
items.answer: Actual growth is an increase in real GDP produced, possibly from using spare capacity; potential growth is an increase in the capacity to produce, from more or better factors of production.
items.markingKey: Actual growth is an increase in real GDP produced, possibly from using spare capacity; potential growth is an increase in the capacity to produce, from more or better factors of production. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly describe Ireland's growth in the 1990s (the "Celtic Tiger") and explain what it reveals about the role of FDI and human capital in growth.
items.answer: Irish real GDP grew at around 6-9% a year in the late 1990s, attracting FDI with a low corporation tax rate, an educated English-speaking workforce and EU single-market access. Foreign firms brought capital and technology while a skilled workforce raised productivity
items.markingKey: Context (Irish real GDP grew at around 6-9% a year in the late 1990s, attracting FDI with a low corporation tax rate, an educated English-speaking workforce and EU single-market access.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: Foreign firms brought capital and technology while a skilled workforce raised productivity – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to the role of FDI and human capital in growth.

items.stem: With the help of a labelled diagram, outline how an increase in the quantity and quality of factors of production leads to long-term economic growth.
items.answer: PPC shifting outward and LRAS (vertical) shifting right from Yp1 to Yp2; explain investment in physical capital, human capital (education, health), technology and institutions.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: PPC shifting outward and LRAS (vertical) shifting right from Yp1 to Yp2; explain investment in physical capital, human capital (education, health), technology and institutions. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: "Countries rich in natural resources always grow faster." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: The "resource curse" shows resource-rich countries can grow slowly because of corruption, volatile prices and Dutch disease; human capital and institutions matter more.
items.markingKey: The "resource curse" shows resource-rich countries can grow slowly because of corruption, volatile prices and Dutch disease; human capital and institutions matter more. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Investment in human capital is the most effective way to achieve long-term economic growth."
items.answer: Human capital is necessary for sustained growth, but it is most effective combined with infrastructure, good institutions and open markets.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: raises productivity of labour; complements technology adoption; reduces inequality and improves health. Arguments against: long time lags; brain drain may export the gains; physical capital and institutions are also required; graduate unemployment if demand for skills is lacking. Supported judgement: Human capital is necessary for sustained growth, but it is most effective combined with infrastructure, good institutions and open markets.

items.stem: Which of the following is a possible negative consequence of rapid economic growth?
options: Demand-pull inflation if AD grows faster than potential output
items.answer: Demand-pull inflation if AD grows faster than potential output
items.markingKey: D. Rapid AD growth can create inflationary gaps.

items.stem: Explain why economic growth may have negative effects on the current account of the balance of payments.
items.answer: Rising incomes increase spending on imports (MPM), so imports may grow faster than exports, worsening the current account balance.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Rising incomes increase spending on imports (MPM), so imports may grow faster than exports, worsening the current account balance. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between economic development and economic growth.
items.answer: Growth is an increase in real output; development is a broader improvement in living standards, including health, education, freedom and reduced poverty.
items.markingKey: Growth is an increase in real output; development is a broader improvement in living standards, including health, education, freedom and reduced poverty. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Kenji writes: "Economic growth always reduces poverty." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Growth can reduce absolute poverty, but if its benefits are unevenly distributed, relative poverty and inequality may rise.
items.markingKey: Growth can reduce absolute poverty, but if its benefits are unevenly distributed, relative poverty and inequality may rise. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Briefly describe income inequality in the USA since 1980 and explain what it reveals about the distributional consequences of growth.
items.answer: The share of US pre-tax national income going to the top 1% roughly doubled from about 10% in 1980 to around 20% in recent years. The gains from growth were concentrated at the top, so median incomes grew much more slowly than average incomes
items.markingKey: Context (The share of US pre-tax national income going to the top 1% roughly doubled from about 10% in 1980 to around 20% in recent years.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of the view that the benefits of economic growth outweigh its costs.
items.answer: Benefits usually outweigh costs for low-income countries, but for all countries the quality (inclusive and sustainable) of growth matters as much as its rate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher incomes and lower absolute poverty; more tax revenue for public services; lower unemployment. Arguments against: environmental degradation and climate change; rising inequality; inflation and current-account pressures; non-renewable resource depletion. Supported judgement: Benefits usually outweigh costs for low-income countries, but for all countries the quality (inclusive and sustainable) of growth matters as much as its rate.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs, through maintaining natural capital"?
items.answer: environmental sustainability

items.stem: Explain why economic growth may not improve living standards for everyone.
items.answer: Growth is an average; if gains are concentrated among high-income groups or regions, many households may see stagnant real incomes, and environmental damage may reduce quality of life.

items.answer: A fall in the level means output is lower than before (negative growth); a fall in the rate means output is still growing but more slowly.

items.stem: Ingrid writes: "Real GDP grew by 3% in 2022 and 3% in 2023, so it grew by exactly 6% over the two years." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Growth compounds: 1.03 × 1.03 = 1.0609, so the total increase is 6.09%.

items.stem:
Read the source below.

Nigeria's real GDP grew by an average of about 2% a year between 2015 and 2023, while its population grew by around 2.5% a year. Over the same period, inflation averaged more than 13% a year.
— Adapted from World Bank data

Using the data, explain what happened to Nigeria's real GDP per capita, and why nominal GDP figures would be misleading.
items.answer: Real GDP per capita fell (≈ 2% − 2.5% = −0.5% a year), so average real incomes declined; nominal GDP rose rapidly because of high inflation, which would wrongly suggest strong growth.
items.markingKey: Real GDP per capita fell (≈ 2% − 2.5% = −0.5% a year), so average real incomes declined; nominal GDP rose rapidly because of high inflation, which would wrongly suggest strong growth. items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "A high rate of economic growth is the best indicator of a successful economy."
items.answer: Growth is important, but success should be judged by sustainable, inclusive growth in real GDP per capita together with other indicators.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher incomes and employment; more resources for public services; easy to measure and compare. Arguments against: may be a rebound from a low base; may come with inflation, inequality or environmental damage; per capita growth matters more than total; stability and sustainability matter too. items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how an increase in the quantity and quality of factors of production leads to long-term economic growth, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: PPC shifting outward and LRAS (vertical) shifting right from Yp1 to Yp2; explain investment in physical capital, human capital (education, health), technology and institutions.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "The benefits of economic growth outweigh its costs."
items.answer: Benefits usually outweigh costs for low-income countries, but for all countries the quality (inclusive and sustainable) of growth matters as much as its rate.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher incomes and lower absolute poverty; more tax revenue for public services; lower unemployment. Arguments against: environmental degradation and climate change; rising inequality; inflation and current-account pressures; non-renewable resource depletion. Supported judgement: Benefits usually outweigh costs for low-income countries, but for all countries the quality (inclusive and sustainable) of growth matters as much as its rate.

items.stem:
Read the extract below.

India's real GDP grew by over 9% in 2021-22 after a 5.8% contraction in 2020-21, then by around 7-8% a year.

Nigeria's real GDP grew by an average of about 2% a year between 2015 and 2023, while its population grew by around 2.5% a year. Over the same period, inflation averaged more than 13% a year.
— Adapted from World Bank data

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that a high rate of economic growth is the best indicator of a successful economy.
items.answer: Growth is important, but success should be judged by sustainable, inclusive growth in real GDP per capita together with other indicators.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: higher incomes and employment; more resources for public services; easy to measure and compare. Arguments against: may be a rebound from a low base; may come with inflation, inequality or environmental damage; per capita growth matters more than total; stability and sustainability matter too. Judgement: Growth is important, but success should be judged by sustainable, inclusive growth in real GDP per capita together with other indicators. Reward explicit use of the extract. items.stem:
Read the extract below.

Ethiopia averaged close to 10% annual growth between 2004 and 2019, driven by public investment in roads, dams and industrial parks.

South Korea's GDP per capita rose from under $200 in 1960 to over $33,000 by 2023, with heavy investment in education, export industries and R&D.

Using information from the extract and your knowledge of economics, evaluate the view that investment in human capital is the most effective way to achieve long-term economic growth.
items.answer: Human capital is necessary for sustained growth, but it is most effective combined with infrastructure, good institutions and open markets.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "An increase in real GDP (or real GDP per capita) over time"?
items.answer: economic growth
items.markingKey: D. This is the definition of economic growth.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "trickle-down effect"?
options: Manufactured resources such as machinery, equipment, buildings and infrastructure used to produce goods and services
Meeting present needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their needs, through maintaining natural capital
The theory that the benefits of growth for high earners eventually spread to lower-income groups through higher spending and employment
Growth in which each period's percentage increase is applied to the previous period's (larger) value
items.answer: The theory that the benefits of growth for high earners eventually spread to lower-income groups through higher spending and employment
items.markingKey: C. "trickle-down effect" is the theory that the benefits of growth for high earners eventually spread to lower-income groups through higher spending and employment.

items.stem: Real GDP per capita growth is approximately equal to:
items.answer: real GDP growth minus population growth
items.markingKey: real GDP growth minus population growth. Per capita growth ≈ g(Y) − g(N).

items.stem: Distinguish between actual economic growth and potential economic growth.
items.answer: Actual growth is an increase in real GDP produced, possibly from using spare capacity; potential growth is an increase in the capacity to produce, from more or better factors of production.
items.markingKey: Actual growth is an increase in real GDP produced, possibly from using spare capacity; potential growth is an increase in the capacity to produce, from more or better factors of production. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Explain why economic growth can improve government finances.
items.answer: Higher incomes and spending raise tax revenues while lower unemployment reduces benefit payments, allowing more spending on public services or lower deficits.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Higher incomes and spending raise tax revenues while lower unemployment reduces benefit payments, allowing more spending on public services or lower deficits. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why growth data for developing countries should be interpreted with caution.
items.answer: Large informal sectors, out-of-date base years, changes in methodology and political pressures can make official real GDP figures inaccurate.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Large informal sectors, out-of-date base years, changes in methodology and political pressures can make official real GDP figures inaccurate. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Leila writes: "Economic growth must always harm the environment." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Growth based on services, renewable energy and efficiency can decouple output from emissions; several high-income countries have cut emissions while growing.
items.markingKey: Growth based on services, renewable energy and efficiency can decouple output from emissions; several high-income countries have cut emissions while growing. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: A student claims that real GDP grew by 3% in 2022 and 3% in 2023, so it grew by exactly 6% over the two years. Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Growth compounds: 1.03 × 1.03 = 1.0609, so the total increase is 6.09%.
items.markingKey: Growth compounds: 1.03 × 1.03 = 1.0609, so the total increase is 6.09%. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Any increase in investment immediately increases potential output." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Investment adds to AD immediately, but it raises potential output only when the new capital becomes productive, and only net of depreciation.
items.markingKey: Investment adds to AD immediately, but it raises potential output only when the new capital becomes productive, and only net of depreciation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Draw a diagram to illustrate how economic growth may lead to negative environmental consequences, using a diagram of negative externalities of production, and outline what it shows.
items.answer: MSC above MPC; market output Qm exceeds socially optimal Q*; welfare loss; explain pollution and resource depletion that accompany growth.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: MSC above MPC; market output Qm exceeds socially optimal Q*; welfare loss; explain pollution and resource depletion that accompany growth. Award up to 2 marks for an accurate, fully labelled diagram and up to 4 for the explanation linked to it.

items.stem: With reference to Ireland's growth in the 1990s (the "Celtic Tiger"), explain how it illustrates the role of FDI and human capital in growth.
items.answer: Irish real GDP grew at around 6-9% a year in the late 1990s, attracting FDI with a low corporation tax rate, an educated English-speaking workforce and EU single-market access. Foreign firms brought capital and technology while a skilled workforce raised productivity

items.stem: Outline one way in which China's poverty reduction since 1980 shows consequences of economic growth for living standards.
items.answer: The World Bank estimates that close to 800 million people in China moved out of extreme poverty between 1980 and 2020. Sustained rapid growth raised incomes and created jobs in manufacturing and services, sharply reducing absolute poverty
